items.label: f01-three-successes
items.front: Name the three layers a Shopify GraphQL mutation must pass before the client records success.
items.back: Transport (an HTTP 200 response), the GraphQL envelope (no top-level errors), and the mutation payload (no userErrors and a created resource ID present).

items.label: f03-hash-not-auth
items.front: What does the plan's hash prove, and what does it not?
items.back: It detects changed normalized content. It is not authorization or a signature, and the preflight is a snapshot: another writer can still change the target after export and before a create.

items.label: f02-timeout-uncertainty
items.front: Why does a mutation timeout stop the migration instead of retrying, while some reads are retried?
items.back: The remote may have committed without returning an ID, so a retry could duplicate or collide on the handle; reads are retried only for selected statuses or throttling, and a fresh export is required after a mutation failure.

items.prompt: A fresh, unedited plan has 3 creates and 1 conflict. What does applyPlan send to the target store?

choices.text: Nothing: any conflict aborts with 'Plan has conflicts; no mutation was sent.'
Only the creates that come before the conflict in the operations array, then it stops
The 3 creates; the conflicting item is skipped and listed in the receipt for review
All 3 creates, plus a placeholder entry for the conflicting item to be fixed later

choices: Nothing: any conflict aborts with 'Plan has conflicts; no mutation was sent.'
Only the creates that come before the conflict in the operations array, then it stops
The 3 creates; the conflicting item is skipped and listed in the receipt for review
All 3 creates, plus a placeholder entry for the conflicting item to be fixed later

items.explanation: The conflict check runs after the staleness check and before the first journal write or mutation.

items.prompt: Someone hand-edits a reviewed plan.json to add an extra createEntry, leaving sourceHash and targetHash untouched, then runs apply. What happens?

choices.text: Apply refuses: it re-exports both stores, rebuilds the plan, and the canonical forms no longer match
Apply runs the extra create, because both sourceHash and targetHash still match the current store exports
Apply skips the hash check whenever the operation count grows, so the edited plan runs in full
Apply runs only the operations it can verify against the hashes and skips the added createEntry

choices: Apply refuses: it re-exports both stores, rebuilds the plan, and the canonical forms no longer match
Apply runs the extra create, because both sourceHash and targetHash still match the current store exports
Apply skips the hash check whenever the operation count grows, so the edited plan runs in full
Apply runs only the operations it can verify against the hashes and skips the added createEntry

items.explanation: The hashes are change detectors, not signatures. Apply compares the whole supplied plan against a freshly rebuilt one, so the plan file cannot become an arbitrary-mutation script.

items.prompt: The target has an entry whose handle does not appear in the source export. What does the plan do with it?

choices.text: Lists it in targetOnly and leaves it alone; a missing source entry is no reason to delete
Copies it back into the source snapshot so the next export and plan include it
Records it as a conflict, which blocks apply until someone decides whether to keep it
Plans a delete for it, so that the target store ends up mirroring the source export exactly

choices: Lists it in targetOnly and leaves it alone; a missing source entry is no reason to delete
Copies it back into the source snapshot so the next export and plan include it
Records it as a conflict, which blocks apply until someone decides whether to keep it
Plans a delete for it, so that the target store ends up mirroring the source export exactly

items.explanation: The planner has no delete operation at all; target-only entries are reported for review and retained.

items.prompt: A definition marks title as required, and a source entry has title set to the empty string. What happens when the snapshot is normalized?

choices.text: It throws 'Required entry field is missing.': an empty string counts as missing
It passes normalization, and the target store rejects the empty title later at create time
It passes, because the title key is present on the entry even though its value is empty
The entry is skipped during normalization and reported in targetOnly for review

choices: It throws 'Required entry field is missing.': an empty string counts as missing
It passes normalization, and the target store rejects the empty title later at create time
It passes, because the title key is present on the entry even though its value is empty
The entry is skipped during normalization and reported in targetOnly for review

items.explanation: A required field must have some value that is neither null nor ''. Validation happens in normalizeSnapshot, before any plan is written.

items.prompt: Apply has created operations 0 and 1; operation 2 fails. What state is left behind?

choices.text: Apply records operation 2 as failed in the receipt and continues with the remaining operations
Creates 0 and 1 stay; the receipt is marked stopped at index 2 and says to re-export before retrying
Apply retries operation 2 with backoff until it succeeds, then finishes the rest of the plan
Creates 0 and 1 are rolled back from the journal, leaving the target store as it was before apply started

choices: Apply records operation 2 as failed in the receipt and continues with the remaining operations
Creates 0 and 1 stay; the receipt is marked stopped at index 2 and says to re-export before retrying
Apply retries operation 2 with backoff until it succeeds, then finishes the rest of the plan
Creates 0 and 1 are rolled back from the journal, leaving the target store as it was before apply started

items.explanation: There is no rollback: the journal is a recovery aid that records confirmed creates. The thrown error carries the in-memory result even if the final journal write fails.

items.prompt: What does buildPlan do when the source and target snapshots name the same store?

choices.text: It logs a warning that both snapshots match and continues planning as usual
It plans creates for every entry, duplicating each one inside the same store
It returns an empty plan with every entry marked unchanged against itself
It throws 'Source and target stores must differ.' before planning anything

choices: It logs a warning that both snapshots match and continues planning as usual
It plans creates for every entry, duplicating each one inside the same store
It returns an empty plan with every entry marked unchanged against itself
It throws 'Source and target stores must differ.' before planning anything

items.explanation: Migrating a store onto itself is refused outright; applyPlan re-checks the same invariant on the clients.

items.prompt: Under canonical(), do { b: 1, a: 2 } and { a: 2, b: 1 } produce the same string? Do [1, 2] and [2, 1]?

choices.text: The objects do, since stable() sorts object keys; the arrays do not, since array order is kept
Both pairs match, because stable() sorts array elements as well as object keys before stringifying
Neither pair matches, because JSON.stringify keeps insertion order for object keys and arrays
The arrays match, because stable() sorts them, but the objects do not, since key order is kept

choices: The objects do, since stable() sorts object keys; the arrays do not, since array order is kept
Both pairs match, because stable() sorts array elements as well as object keys before stringifying
Neither pair matches, because JSON.stringify keeps insertion order for object keys and arrays
The arrays match, because stable() sorts them, but the objects do not, since key order is kept

items.explanation: stable maps arrays element-wise without sorting and rebuilds objects from Object.keys(value).sort(). Order-insensitive collections are sorted explicitly in normalizeSnapshot instead (by key, handle, type).

items.prompt: Planning the example fixtures against an empty target yields one createDefinition and one createEntry. Why must they appear in that order?

choices.text: The entry's type does not exist in the target until its definition is created, and apply runs in order
Operations are sorted alphabetically by kind, which happens to put createDefinition before createEntry
createDefinition must come first so the receipt's indices line up with the order of the sourceHash
applyPlan runs operations in parallel, so the order only matters for how the plan reads to a reviewer

choices: The entry's type does not exist in the target until its definition is created, and apply runs in order
Operations are sorted alphabetically by kind, which happens to put createDefinition before createEntry
createDefinition must come first so the receipt's indices line up with the order of the sourceHash
applyPlan runs operations in parallel, so the order only matters for how the plan reads to a reviewer

items.explanation: buildPlan pushes createDefinition before looping over that definition's entries, and applyPlan iterates current.operations by index.

items.prompt: The target already has an entry with the same handle as a source entry, but one field value differs. What does buildPlan do with it?

choices.text: Plans an update operation that overwrites the target's value with the differing source value
Plans a createEntry under a suffixed handle such as handle-2, so both versions are kept
Records a conflict: 'Existing entry differs; update policy must be reviewed.'
Marks it unchanged, since the handle is the entry's identity and matching handles are enough

choices: Plans an update operation that overwrites the target's value with the differing source value
Plans a createEntry under a suffixed handle such as handle-2, so both versions are kept
Records a conflict: 'Existing entry differs; update policy must be reviewed.'
Marks it unchanged, since the handle is the entry's identity and matching handles are enough

items.explanation: A matching handle is compared canonically: equal goes to unchanged, different goes to conflicts. The utility only creates missing content.

items.prompt: A source entry has an optional field whose value is null. How does that field appear in the planned createEntry input?

choices.text: It is sent with an explicit null so that the target store clears the field value
It is converted to an empty string, since create input accepts text only
The whole entry is rejected as incomplete and listed among the conflicts
It is left out: fields whose value is null are filtered from the create input

choices: It is sent with an explicit null so that the target store clears the field value
It is converted to an empty string, since create input accepts text only
The whole entry is rejected as incomplete and listed among the conflicts
It is left out: fields whose value is null are filtered from the create input

items.explanation: The input is built with entry.fields.filter((f) => f.value !== null).map(({ key, value })); the field type is dropped too, since create input takes key/value only.

items.prompt: A source definition has one product_reference field among several text fields. How does buildPlan treat that definition?

choices.text: It creates the definition and copies the source store's product IDs into the target store as-is
It creates the definition and sets every reference value to null until IDs can be mapped
It creates the definition without the reference field and plans the text fields as usual
The whole definition becomes a conflict, since reference fields need cross-store ID mapping

choices: It creates the definition and copies the source store's product IDs into the target store as-is
It creates the definition and sets every reference value to null until IDs can be mapped
It creates the definition without the reference field and plans the text fields as usual
The whole definition becomes a conflict, since reference fields need cross-store ID mapping

items.explanation: Any field whose type includes 'reference' blocks the definition with an explicit reason; a source-store product ID is meaningless in the target store.
